part_title: AI Fundamentals, Use Cases and Rule-Based vs Learning Systems
review_basis: Original AIF Module 03 WebP slides 01–08 personally reviewed; each narrative follows visible flow, labels and worked examples.

scenes.title: AI definitions and scope
scenes.narration: Look at the diagram from left to right. On the far left are the things an AI system may receive: text, images, audio, video or other data. Data is information represented in a form a computer can process. In the central box, the slide shows perception, learning, reasoning, and decision or generation. Perception means identifying useful information in the input. Learning means finding patterns from examples. Reasoning means applying available information or rules to a task. The output might be a classification, a prediction, an action or newly generated content. This diagram is a general overview, not a claim that every AI system uses all four stages in exactly this order. Now look at the four definitions along the bottom. Artificial intelligence is the broad field. Machine learning is a subset of AI that learns patterns from data. Deep learning is a subset of machine learning that commonly uses neural networks with multiple layers. Generative AI focuses on generating new content such as text, images, sound or code, and many current generative systems use deep learning. An AI model is the computational system performing a task; it is not a human mind. Take a college help desk. Predicting which department should answer a student query is classification. Writing a draft reply is generation. A rule such as 'all applications close at midnight' might simply be programmed. We should select the simplest safe approach that satisfies the business requirement. The decision cue at the bottom asks when to use generative AI: when creating new content is central to the task. Quick check: a system that predicts next year's enrollment from historical data is typically solving a prediction problem, not necessarily a generative-writing task.

scenes.title: AI use cases: choose the capability
scenes.narration: This visual shows four AI capabilities, each matching a different kind of input and goal. First, computer vision: the factory-image panel distinguishes a normal metal component from one with a defect. Computer vision uses image or video data to identify visual patterns. Amazon Rekognition is one AWS-managed computer-vision service, but detecting specialized manufacturing defects may require an appropriate custom model or dedicated vision solution. Second, facial recognition compares facial features in images. The illustration shows a sample high match percentage. A number like ninety-nine point eight percent is not proof of identity, and real use needs strong privacy, consent, bias testing, security and human review where appropriate. Third, fraud detection. The payment example includes an amount, location, time and merchant, and the system flags the unusual transaction for review. A fraud alert is a risk signal, not automatic proof someone committed fraud. Fourth, intelligent document processing. Follow the invoice on the right into structured fields such as invoice number, date, items and total. Amazon Textract can extract text, tables and forms from documents. Extracting information is a different task from generating a new policy or paragraph. At the bottom, the decision guide matches images with computer vision, identity comparison with face matching, unusual financial behavior with anomaly detection, and invoices with document extraction. Consider a university office with hundreds of forms. Would you begin by writing a chatbot to invent answers, or by extracting the actual data from each form and validating it? Document extraction and validation are the more direct starting point. Always consider false matches, incorrect extraction and personal data safeguards before deploying.

scenes.title: AI solution components and practitioner roles
scenes.narration: An AI project requires more than a model. This slide separates the solution into four connected layers. On the left is the data layer. Here we gather and prepare suitable examples such as photos, documents or records. A data scientist may inspect missing values, errors, bias and whether the examples represent the actual problem. The next box is the machine-learning framework and algorithm layer. An algorithm is a procedure for learning from examples; a framework is software that helps people build and run the process. Specialists choose an approach, run experiments and evaluate performance. Third is the model layer, which contains the learned structure, parameters and training or optimization process. Parameters are numeric values adjusted during training; the optimizer helps change them to reduce mistakes. Fourth is the application layer, where a developer integrates the working model into software that ordinary people use. Follow the photo-organizer example below. First we collect pictures. Next we choose an appropriate image-recognition method. Then a model learns patterns associated with people, places and objects. Finally an application lets users search their photos. Notice the different skills involved: a data scientist studies the data and metrics, an ML engineer helps develop and deploy models, and a software developer delivers the experience to users. In real teams these responsibilities overlap, especially in smaller organizations. A student does not need to master every specialist role just to understand the AI Practitioner foundations. A practical decision question: if your model predicts correctly in a notebook but the website never displays the prediction, which layer should you investigate first? The application integration and deployment layer, while also checking that the model endpoint is reachable.

scenes.title: What is Machine Learning (ML)?
scenes.narration: Machine learning is a way of creating predictions or decisions from patterns found in data. Follow the top four-stage picture. First is training data: the illustrated photos already have labels such as mountain, beach and forest. A label is the known category assigned to an example. The learning process examines many examples, using an algorithm to adjust the model so it can distinguish patterns. The resulting trained model stores those learned relationships. On the far right a new image arrives, and the model predicts mountain. Using a trained model on a new input is called inference. This is different from training it again. Now compare the two panels at the bottom. Regression predicts a numeric value. The example estimates a home's price at five hundred twenty thousand dollars from characteristics such as location and size. That number is an illustrative prediction, not a guaranteed sale price. Classification chooses a category. The email example predicts spam rather than not spam. Both are common supervised learning tasks when examples include correct labels. The system still needs evaluation on new examples, because training accuracy alone does not prove it will perform well on real-world inputs. A model can make errors, learn biases from the data or become less accurate as conditions change. Imagine a college predicting how many students will enroll next year: a numeric prediction resembles regression. Sorting incoming applications into departments resembles classification. Quick check: does machine learning require developers to manually write every pattern such as every possible spam phrase? No. The model learns useful relationships from examples, though developers still choose data, algorithms, goals and safety checks.

scenes.title: AI includes rule-based expert systems
scenes.narration: This slide corrects an important misunderstanding: artificial intelligence is broader than machine learning. The large umbrella covers at least two illustrated approaches. On the left are rule-based expert systems. A human expert writes explicit instructions, often in an if-then form. For example, if an invoice total differs from the sum of its line items, then send the invoice for review. The middle example shows line items of one hundred, two hundred and one hundred fifty dollars, totaling four hundred fifty, but the invoice declares five hundred. The system can flag the fifty-dollar mismatch using arithmetic and a clear rule. No training dataset is required to discover this rule. On the right are machine-learning models, which learn patterns from labeled or unlabeled data and use learned parameters to predict new outcomes. The fraud example learns from transactions previously labeled as fraud or legitimate. This is useful when suspicious patterns are too varied for a manageable fixed rule list. The historic MYCIN example at the lower left was a research expert system that used many human-authored rules for infectious-disease reasoning. It was a research demonstration, not a replacement for clinicians or routine medical care. A rule-based program can explain which conditions triggered an output, but its rules might be incomplete or outdated. A machine-learning model may adapt to complex patterns but must be evaluated for false alarms, missed cases and fairness. Many practical systems combine these approaches: a fraud model provides a score and business rules decide when a person should review the transaction. Test your understanding: if a university policy states that forms submitted after a fixed deadline must be marked late, do we need to train a model? No. An explicit rule may be more transparent and dependable.
